{{Short description|British grammarian and linguist}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2017}} {{Use British English|date=August 2017}} {{Infobox scientist | name = Rodney Desmond Huddleston | birth_date = {{birth date and age|df=y|1937|4|4}} | birth_place = [[Bowdon, Cheshire]], England | citizenship = {{Plainlist| * British * Australian}} | workplaces = {{Plainlist| * [[University of Queensland]] (1967–1997) * [[University of Reading]] (1967–1968) * [[University of London]] (1964–1967, 1968–1969) * [[University of Edinburgh]] (1963–1964)}} | alma_mater = {{Plainlist| * [[Cambridge University]] (B.A.) * [[University of Edinburgh]] (PhD)}} | thesis_title = Descriptive and comparative analysis of text in French and English | thesis_url = https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/17537 | thesis_year = 1963 | doctoral_advisor = [[Michael Halliday]] | doctoral_students = Francis Bond | known_for = {{Plainlist| * ''[[The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language]]''}} | awards = {{Plainlist| * [[Leonard Bloomfield Book Award]] (2004; shared with [[Geoff Pullum]]) * Fellow, Australian Academy of the Humanities, awarded a Personal Chair * 'Excellence in Teaching' award * Centenary Medal for service to Australian society and the humanities in the study of linguistics}} | website = {{Official URL}} | spouse = {{Plainlist| * Joan Mulholland (1965–78) * Cheryll Jacklin (1978-1985) * Vivienne Pool (1988–)}} }} '''Rodney D. Huddleston''' (born 4 April 1937) is a British [[linguistics|linguist]] and [[Linguist|grammarian]] specializing in the study and description of English. Huddleston is the primary author of ''[[The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language]]'' ({{ISBN|0-521-43146-8}}), which presents a comprehensive [[grammar|descriptive grammar]] of English. == Early life and education == Huddleston was born in [[Cheshire]], England, and attended [[Manchester Grammar School]]. Upon leaving school, he spent two years in the military completing [[National Service]] before enrolling at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]], with a scholarship, where he graduated in 1960 with a First Class Honours degree in Modern and Medieval Languages.'Cambridge Tripos Results', ''Times'', 20 June 1960, p. 20. After graduating from Cambridge, Huddleston earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in Applied Linguistics{{Cite web |last=R. D. |first=Huddleston |date=1963 |title=Descriptive and comparative analysis of text in French and English |url=http://hdl.handle.net/1842/17537 |language=en |hdl=1842/17537}} from the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1963 under the supervision of [[Michael Halliday]].{{cite book |editor-last1=Collins |editor-first1=Peter |editor-last2=Lee |editor-first2=David |title=The Clause in English: In Honour of Rodney Huddleston |date=1999 |publisher=John Benjamins Publishing |location=Amsterdam, Netherlands |page=xvii |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2jGMEHkq7zwC&pg=PR17 |chapter=Curriculum Vitae of Rodney Desmond Huddleston |series=Studies in Language Companion Series |volume=45 |isbn=978-90-272-3048-5 |issn=0165-7763 |lccn=98-39788 |oclc=39695769}} == Academic career == Huddleston held lectureships at the [[University of Edinburgh]], [[University College London]], and the [[University of Reading]]. In 1969, he moved to the University of Queensland, where he remained for the rest of his career. He was the recipient of the first round of 'Excellence in Teaching' awards at the University of Queensland in 1988. In 1990, he was awarded a Personal Chair.{{Cite book|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=RFtYPgAACAAJ|title = The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language: About the Author|date = 25 April 2002|access-date = 19 August 2015|isbn = 9780521527613|last1 = Huddleston|first1 = Rodney|last2 = Pullum|first2 = Geoffrey K.| publisher=Cambridge University Press }} He is currently an [[emeritus professor]] at the [[University of Queensland]], where he taught until 1997. === Under Halliday === For some time, Huddleston ran a project under Halliday in the Communications Research Centre at The University of London called the “OSTI Programme in the Linguistic Properties of Scientific English.”{{Cite book |last=O'Donnell |first=Mick |url=http://www.isfla.org/Systemics/History/HallidayLifePart1-2-vOct08.pdf |title=Life of Michael Alexander Kirkwook Halliday: A Personal Biography}} (OSTI was the [[Government of the United Kingdom|UK government]]'s Office for Scientific and Technical Information.){{Cite book |last1=Sinclair |first1=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1kTkHAXeL3IC&pg=PR4 |title=English Collocation Studies: The OSTI Report |last2=Jones |first2=Susan |last3=Daley |first3=Robert |date=2004-09-22 |publisher=A&C Black |isbn=978-0-8264-7489-6 |language=en}} As a student of Halliday's, Huddleston was a proponent of [[Systemic functional grammar|Systemic Functional Grammar]], but as his thinking developed, he came to reject it.{{Cite journal |last=Huddleston |first=Rodney |date=1988 |title=Constituency, multi-functionality and grammaticalization in Halliday's Functional Grammar |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0022226700011592/type/journal_article |journal=Journal of Linguistics |language=en |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=137–174 |doi=10.1017/S0022226700011592 |s2cid=145197674 |issn=0022-2267|url-access=subscription }} === ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'' === ==== Background ==== In 1988, Huddleston published a very critical review of the 1985 book ''[[A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language]]''.{{Cite journal |last=Huddleston |first=Rodney |date=1988 |title=''A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language'' by Randolph Quirk, Sidney Greenbaum, Geoffrey Leech, Jan Svartvik |url=http://archive.org/details/comprehensivegra00englrich |journal=Language |volume=64 |pages=345–354 |doi=10.2307/415437 |jstor=415437}} He wrote:
[T]here are some respects in which it is seriously flawed and disappointing. A number of quite basic categories and concepts do not seem to have been thought through with sufficient care; this results in a remarkable amount of unclarity and inconsistency in the analysis, and in the organization of the grammar.
A year later, he decided that he would have to produce a grammar that did a better job. He was awarded a special projects grant by The University of Queensland to the project and began work on what was provisionally titled ''The Cambridge Grammar of English''.The eventual title – whose obvious abbreviation ''CGEL'' was already in wide use for ''[[A Comprehensive Grammar of the English Language]]'' – was imposed by [[Cambridge University Press|the publisher]]. {{Cite web |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |date=29 July 2002 |title=Some points of agreement about the Cambridge Grammar |url=https://old.linguistlist.org/issues/13/13-2005.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308060237/https://old.linguistlist.org/issues/13/13-2005.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=8 March 2023 |access-date=8 March 2023 |work=Linguist List |number=13.2005}} From 1989 to 1995, workshops were held two or three times a year in Brisbane and Sydney to develop ideas for the framework and content.{{Cite book |last1=Pullum |first1=Geoffrey K. |title=The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language |last2=Huddleston |first2=Rodney |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-43146-8 |editor-last1=Huddleston |editor-first1=Rodney |location=Cambridge |pages=xv–xvii |chapter=Preface |editor-last2=Pullum |editor-first2=Geoffrey K.}}
Intellectually, these were intense and exhausting sessions but they were associated with extremely enjoyable social gatherings. In some ways it is the social side of these events that lingers in the memory long after the details of linguistic discussion are forgotten. We remember particularly dawn jogs to Alexandra Beach from Rodney’s house at Sunshine Beach, pool volleyball and table tennis games fought with great ferocity, and walks through Noosa National Park with spectacular sunsets over Noosa Bay.{{Rp|page=xi}}
[[Geoff Pullum]] joined the project in 1995,{{Cite journal |last=Culicover |first=Peter W. |date=2004 |title=none |department=Review of ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'' |journal=Language |language=en |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=127–141 |doi=10.1353/lan.2004.0018 |issn=1535-0665 |s2cid=140478848 |authorlink=Peter Culicover}} Also a [https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/culicover.1/Publications/CGEL_Review.pdf preprint] (with different pagination). after Huddleston "bemoaned the problems he was having in maintaining the momentum of this huge project, at that time already five years underway".{{Cite journal |last=Crystal |first=David |date=2002 |title=Indexing aids |url=http://www.davidcrystal.com/Files/BooksAndArticles/-4092.pdf |department=Review of ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'' |journal=The Indexer |volume=23 |pages=108–109 |authorlink=David Crystal}} ==== Publication and reception ==== The book was published in 2002. In 2004, [[Peter Culicover]] wrote:
''The Cambridge grammar of the English language'' (''CGEL'') is a monumentally impressive piece of work. Already published reviews of this work do not overstate its virtues: 'a notable achievement'; 'authoritative, interesting, reasonably priced (for a book of this size), beautifully designed, well proofread, and enjoyable to handle'; 'superbly produced and designed'; 'one of the most superb works of academic scholarship ever to appear on the English linguistics scene ... a monumental work that offers easily the most comprehensive and thought-provoking treatment of English grammar to date. Nothing rivals this work, with respect to breadth, depth and consistency of coverage'. I fully agree with these sentiments. Huddleston, Pullum, and collaborators definitely deserve a prize for this achievement.{{Cite journal |last=Culicover |first=Peter W. |date=2004 |title=none |department=Review of ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'' |journal=Language |language=en |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=127–141 |doi=10.1353/lan.2004.0018 |issn=1535-0665 |s2cid=140478848 |authorlink=Peter Culicover}} Also a [https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/culicover.1/Publications/CGEL_Review.pdf preprint] (with different pagination).{{Rp|page=127}}
That same year, the book won the [[Leonard Bloomfield Book Award]] of the [[Linguistic Society of America]].{{Cite web |title=Leonard Bloomfield Book Award Previous Holders |url=http://www.linguisticsociety.org/content/leonard-bloomfield-book-award-previous-holders |access-date=August 18, 2015 |website=Linguistic Society of America}} == Views == Huddleston's grammatical frameworks, such as that in the ''Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'', have been monotonic [[Phrase structure grammar|phrase-structure grammars]], similar to [[X-bar theory]] but with explicit notation for [[Grammatical relation|syntactic functions]] such as subject, modifier, and complement.{{Cite book |last1=Pullum |first1=Geoffrey K. |url=http://www.lel.ed.ac.uk/~gpullum/EssexLAGB.pdf |title=Annual Meeting of the Linguistics Association of Great Britain |last2=Rogers |first2=James |year=2009 |pages=1–16 |chapter=Expressive power of the syntactic theory implicit in The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language}} Monotonic phrase-structure grammars are based on the idea that the structure of sentences can be represented as a hierarchy of constituents, with each level of the hierarchy corresponding to a different level of grammatical organization. X-bar theory is a specific type of phrase-structure grammar that posits a uniform structure for all phrasal categories, with each phrase containing a "head" and optional specifier and/or complement. The key difference between monotonic phrase-structure grammars and generative grammars like transformational-generative grammar (TGG) is the absence of transformations or movement operations in the former. Monotonic grammars maintain that the structure of a sentence remains fixed from its initial formation, whereas generative grammars propose that sentences can undergo various transformations during the derivation process. He believes that some kind of fusion of functions accounts for noun phrases that lack noun heads.{{Cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=John |last2=Huddleston |first2=Rodney |last3=Pullum |first3=Geoffrey K. |year=2007 |title=Fusion of functions: The syntax of ''once'', ''twice'' and ''thrice'' |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/s002222670700477x |journal=Journal of Linguistics |publication-date=2007 |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=565–603 |doi=10.1017/s002222670700477x |issn=0022-2267 |s2cid=145799573|url-access=subscription }} === Other === In 1999, a ''{{lang|de|[[Wiktionary: festschrift|festschrift]]}}'' volume was produced "by colleagues past and present, friends and admirers of Rodney Huddleston, in order to honour his consistently outstanding contribution to grammatical theory and description": ''The Clause in English: In Honour of Rodney Huddleston''.{{Cite book|title = The Clause in English: In Honour of Rodney Huddleston|last = Collins|first = Peter and David A. Lee|publisher = John Benjamins Publishing|year = 1999}} Huddleston and his wife Vivienne now reside on [[Sunshine Coast, Queensland|Sunshine Coast]], near Noosa Heads in [[Sunshine Coast, Queensland|Queensland]], [[Australia]].{{Cite web|title = A Student's Introduction to English Grammar|url = http://www.lel.ed.ac.uk/~gpullum/SIEG/authors.html|website = www.lel.ed.ac.uk|access-date = 2015-10-18}}{{Cite book|title = Contemporary Authors, New Revision Series v. 141|year = 2006|pages = 219–221|url = http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3417700103.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160224231439/https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3417700103.html|url-status = dead|archive-date = 2016-02-24}} == Notes == {{reflist|group=n}} == References == {{Reflist}} == Partial bibliography == * Huddleston, Rodney D.
